name: Color analysis

lead: Color analysis assigns you a palette, traditionally one of four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter), based on your skin undertone, hair and eye colour. The payoff people want is a clearer, brighter-looking complexion and a more harmonious face, simply from wearing the colours that sit best next to it.

The chain is direct: colours worn near the face reflect onto skin and change how it reads, so the right shade can make skin look healthier and the wrong one can make it look sallow. The method was popularised in the early 1980s and went viral on TikTok in the early 2020s. Studies have found people prefer clothing hues that harmonise with their skin tone, while the specific season categories have little peer-reviewed validation.

paras: Practitioners hold coloured fabric near the face, usually in daylight, and judge how it affects skin, eyes and contrast. Results are then turned into a palette for tops, scarves, makeup and hair colour. Variants expand the four seasons into twelve or more sub-seasons by adding undertone, lightness and chroma. The effect of a colour is visible immediately, so many people simply test shades in a mirror.

There is no physical risk. Costs come from paid consultations and from buying new clothes to fit a palette. Different analysts and apps can assign the same person to different seasons, and early systems were criticised for centring white clients.

web.title: Clothing Aesthetics: Consistent Colour Choices to Match Fair and Tanned Skin Tones

angle.text: You get sorted into a palette based on skin undertone, hair and eyes, then wear those colours and makeup shades near your face so your complexion looks brighter and healthier. The effect of a colour shows up the moment you hold it up. Studies show people prefer clothing hues that harmonise with their skin tone.

lead: Color analysis, also called seasonal or personal color analysis, is a styling method that advises people which clothing, makeup and hair colours suit them, based on skin, hair and eye colouring. People use it to look clearer-skinned, brighter-eyed and more harmonious by wearing shades matched to their own colouring, which makes it one of the cheapest appearance upgrades discussed in style and looksmaxxing circles [1][2].

Most systems sort people into four seasons (winter, spring, summer, autumn) with sub-variants, usually by undertone (cool blue versus warm yellow), lightness and contrast between hair, skin and eyes [1][2]. The modern consumer version was popularised by consultant Carole Jackson's 1980 book Color Me Beautiful, drawing on earlier work by Johannes Itten, Robert Dorr and Suzanne Caygill, and it went viral again on TikTok in the 2020s [1][2][3].

Published research is small. A 2021 study at the University of St Andrews found that observers tended to match bluer clothing to fair skin and orange-red clothing to tanned skin, a pattern that fits the idea that skin tone guides flattering colour choice [4]. Encyclopedia summaries also record reported inconsistencies between different analysis systems [1][2].
infobox: Four seasons; extended systems of 12 or more sub-seasons [1][2]
Draping fabric swatches near the face; online quizzes and apps [2]

paras: Practitioners assess skin undertone (warm, cool or neutral), value (lightness or depth) and chroma (brightness or muting), together with hair and eye colour [3]. In the classic four-season model, winters are described as suiting rich saturated shades, summers softer muted tones, springs bright warm colours and autumns earthy hues [2].

The usual technique is draping: fabric swatches are held near the face, ideally in daylight because artificial light can shift how colours appear, to see how each shade affects skin and eyes [3]. At-home variants include comparing white fabrics or gold versus silver jewellery, and wrist-vein checks [3]. Wikipedia notes that many systems treat skin tone as the deciding factor and regard it as fixed over a lifetime, even after tanning [1].

Followers apply the palette to everyday clothing near the face (tops, scarves, collars), to foundation and lipstick shades, and to hair colour. The stated aim is to look healthier and more vibrant with no change to the face itself, which is why it appears alongside makeup, grooming and wardrobe advice in style-focused looksmaxxing discussion [3].

Michel Eugène Chevreul's 19th-century work on colour contrast and Albert Munsell's hue, value and chroma system supplied the vocabulary later used by analysts [1]. Johannes Itten linked personal colouring to the four seasons in his teaching and in his 1961 book The Art of Color [1][3]. Robert Dorr developed the Color Key System separating cool-undertone and warm-undertone groups, and Suzanne Caygill published Color: The Essence of You in 1980 after running a San Francisco salon from 1945 [1][3].

Cheaper colour printing in the 1970s and 1980s enabled mass-market books by Bernice Kentner and Carole Jackson [1]. Jackson's Color Me Beautiful (1980) became a bestseller; the Washington Post reported her company grossed 2.5 million dollars in 1982 [2]. In 2000 Kathryn Kalisz introduced the twelve-palette Sci\ART system [3]. Social-media tutorials and AI colour apps spread the practice further in the 2010s and 2020s [1][3].

A 2007 University of Huddersfield thesis by T. Cassidy compared three personal colour analysis systems and reported inconsistencies: although they claimed to use hue, saturation and value, many palettes relied on two of the three [1]. The 2021 i-Perception study by Perrett and Sprengelmeyer asked 96 and 75 participants to choose clothing colours for photographs of fair and tanned White women; observers chose blue hues more often for fair skin and orange-red hues for tanned skin, and the authors argued a blue-yellow colour measure explained choices somewhat better than a simple warm/cool split. They noted that the faces were all young White women and that testing was online [4].

Wikipedia also describes a recent study of lipstick categories used by Japanese Instagram influencers, in which warm and cool categories matched measurable colour traits better than the four-season scheme [1]. Critics quoted in encyclopedia coverage say the four categories simplify continuous variation in pigmentation, that no standard qualification exists for analysts and that fees vary widely; the original book was also criticised for focusing mainly on white clients [1][2][3]. Independent tests have found that different apps can assign the same person to different seasons [3].

No studies found. No clinical trial has tested whether wearing a personally assigned seasonal palette changes perceived attractiveness. Perception studies of skin tone and clothing colour preference exist and are described above [4].
